Retour vers le présent de la réconciliat: Back to the Present of Reconciliation
Table ronde à l’UQAM : témoignages autoc: A roundtable at UQAM: Indigenous voices on reconciliation, language, land and resilience.
Une activiste autochtone tient une plume: An Indigenous activist holds a feather in front of the statue of John A. Macdonald. Photo credit: Pablo Ortiz
Aujourd’hui, nous soulignons la Journée: Today, we mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. It is a day to remember the children from Indigenous communities who never came home from residential schools, and to honour the survivors and their families.
Hier, j’ai assisté à une table ronde org: Yesterday, I attended a roundtable on the theme “Reconciliation from Yesterday to Today.” It was organized by NISKA, a space for UQAM’s Indigenous student community. Ten years after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada released its report, the stories shared there moved me deeply. They are a reminder of how painful the past has been and how it lingers today, but also of how strong resilience is.
Parler de réconciliation, c’est aussi pa: Talking about reconciliation also means talking about language, land and identity. These voices made me want to learn to listen differently.
N’hésitez pas à porter un chandail orang: Don’t hesitate to wear an orange shirt today!
<strong>Lundi 29 septembre, 12 h.</stron: Monday, September 29, noon. The room at UQAM slowly fills up. Students, professors and members of the public from all walks of life take their seats. Many wear orange shirts, a symbol of remembrance and solidarity with survivors of Indigenous residential schools. The atmosphere is attentive: people are here to listen, to learn and to reflect.
Au cœur de cette table ronde intitulée «: At the heart of this roundtable, titled “Reconciliation from Yesterday to Today” and organized by NISKA, a student initiative for Indigenous people at UQAM, four women with remarkable life stories take the floor. They are Pascale O’Bomsawin, an Abenaki language teacher; Caroline Nepton Hotte; Véronique Basile Hébert, an Atikamekw theatre artist from the community of Wemotaci; and the Innu poet Joséphine Bacon.
Ensemble, elles partagent leurs perspect: Together, they share their perspectives and their own journeys of reconciliation, 10 years after the publication of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada’s report. Above all, they ask what it concretely means to “reconcile” today.
Chaque 30 septembre, la Journée national: Every September 30, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation pays tribute to the children who never came home, as well as to residential school survivors and their families. From 1831 to 1996, some 150,000 Inuit, Métis and First Nations children were torn from their families and sent to nearly 130 residential schools across Canada. In the wake of class-action lawsuits, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada travelled the country for six years, gathering thousands of testimonies. Its report, published in 2015, set out 94 calls to action. The preface sets the tone from the start: “Getting to the truth was hard, but getting to reconciliation will be harder.”
C’est précisément cette tension qui anim: It is precisely this tension that drives the gathering at UQAM. “I hope we really do reconcile,” Joséphine Bacon says with a little laugh. But the word itself is already up for debate.
Pour Véronique Basile Hébert, le terme «: For Véronique Basile Hébert, the term “reconciliation” remains too politically loaded. “Was there ever conciliation before we started talking about reconciliation? I think there were some interesting moments of conciliation (...) In 1701, we had the <l1>Great Peace of Montréal treaty.</l1> I think there was a moment of conciliation, an attempt at conciliation, back then. But was that really what we wanted, for it to last over time? Or was it just to calm tempers on one side or the other until someone could get the upper hand? [...] Personally, I’d rather talk about conciliation than reconciliation, because there’s a political dimension to how that term is used. Conciliation of needs, of diverging interests…” she says, sceptical.
“Reconciling sounds like forgiving. But forgiving whom? And above all… is the other side [supposed] to forgive you?” – Joséphine Bacon
Chez d’autres, c’est carrément la colère: For others, the word stirs up outright anger. Joséphine Bacon, who grew up in a residential school, picks up the thread: “We, the people of my generation, started getting angry when people started talking about healing, about reconciliation. That’s when we began to think about what we had really been through in those schools.”
Elle poursuit en puisant dans ses souven: She goes on, drawing on her memories. “I remember the former students paid tribute to Father Laurent, from the Maliotenam residential school. I don’t know how to explain it, but we weren’t angry. And yet we saw our parents every 10 months. When we got back to our families, we were like strangers. And just when we were starting to feel at ease with our families again, it was time to go back to the residential school. These are the things that come back to me. I thought about that party we threw for Father Laurent. We weren’t angry. Everyone who had gone to the residential school was there…” the poet recalls.
Après un long silence, elle reprend : «: After a long silence, she continues: “Reconciling sounds like forgiving. But forgiving whom? And above all… is the other side [supposed] to forgive you?” Coming from her, the word takes on a painful resonance. “Reconciliation made us think about what had really happened to us at the residential school...”
<strong>« Comment pouvons-nous faire ava: “How can we move the Canadian reconciliation process forward without talking about the land?”
À ce débat sur les mots, Caroline Nepton: To this debate over words, Caroline Nepton Hotte adds another dimension: the connection to the land. “How can we move the Canadian reconciliation process forward without talking about the land?” she asks. For her, reconciliation cannot be imagined in a vacuum. It has to go through the land, Indigenous knowledge and the living relationships that surround us.
M<sup>me</sup> Nepton Hotte évoque ses m: M<sup>s</sup> Nepton Hotte describes her walks in the forest: the ancient mosses, the berries, the medicinal plants. “We call them natural resources,” she says. “But are they really resources? Or are they the life around us?” Here, reconciliation takes root in concrete things. She notably mentions Bill 97 on forest management, which has now been put on ice. In that fight, land defenders mobilized to protect the caribou, the rivers and the forests. “We managed to stop that bill, but it’s only a reprieve. There’s still an enormous amount of work to do,” she stresses. “A lot on our plate,” she adds with a laugh, before reminding the audience that the unbridled exploitation of the land remains a crucial issue.
Puis la parole glisse vers une autre for: The conversation then turns to another heritage that needs safeguarding: language. For Pascale O’Bomsawin, this is where it all begins. Yet the language was never passed down to her. “My grandfather spoke Abenaki, but my father didn’t. So I felt a responsibility to reclaim it. I wanted to understand why certain things hurt me in everyday life, why I felt out of place,” she says.
« Il y a 10 ans, je côtoyais des aînés a: “Ten years ago, I was spending time with Anishinaabe elders who were starting to offer Anishinaabemowin classes. I signed up. When I introduced myself, the elder said to me: ‘What are you doing here? Go learn your own language!’” she recounts, laughing.
« Quand j’ai voulu réellement apprendre: “When I really wanted to learn my language, it was a non-Indigenous person who taught me the advanced basics. In my community, there was no one left who could guide me at that level. If a non-Indigenous person hadn’t chosen to learn a language of this land rather than a foreign language, the chain would have been broken,” she points out.
M<sup>me</sup> O’Bomsawin sonne l’alarme: M<sup>s</sup> O’Bomsawin is sounding the alarm. “If you think Indigenous languages are doing well, they’re not! I’ve just come out of three days of meetings with the regional committee on ancestral languages, and the situation is worrying.”
Selon l’Organisation des Nations unies (: According to the United Nations (UN), an average of two Indigenous languages disappear every month, and 40% of the world’s languages, most of them Indigenous, are at risk of eventually dying out for lack of speakers.
Son histoire illustre pourtant la force: Yet her story shows the power of transmission picking back up. “What’s special about my process of reconciliation and healing is that a year ago, my father came to my beginner Abenaki class to break that cycle of being stripped of our identity. He told himself: ‘I’m going to take Abenaki classes. But there’s no way I’m learning it from anyone other than my daughter!’” she says proudly.
Portés par le thème « Réconciliation d’h: Guided by the theme “Reconciliation from Yesterday to Today,” the discussion turns to the future: it is about healing, but also about recognizing that this process cannot be done alone. “Learn to be allies,” Pascale O’Bomsawin urges. “We talk about reconciling with ourselves, but we also have to reconcile with society. And who is society? It’s everyone. It takes two to tango, and it takes two to reconcile. Yes, there’s reconciliation with yourself, with the land, with our identity, but there’s also reconciliation with the other.”
Elle poursuit : « Souvent, les gens me d: She continues: “People often tell me, ‘Pascale, I know absolutely nothing about all this.’ But that’s perfect! You’ve just realized that you don’t know anything. So in that curiosity, make room for yourselves to learn and to make mistakes. Because we make them too.”
